AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND CONTEXT
AbstractText.content: The available evidence regarding low back pain (LBP) incident episodes is not consistent. Such knowledge can add information for the potential contribution of preventive programs.

AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: a) To evaluate annual incident episodes of LBP among the general population. b) To evaluate the contribution of demographic, lifestyle, and back pain history to LBP incident episodes.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENT SAMPLE
AbstractText.content: A randomized sample of individuals, free of LBP at a previous cross-sectional survey.

AbstractText.Label: OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Low back pain during the past year.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Subjects were followed up after 1 year. Baseline data included back pain history, perception of general health, physical activity, smoking, work satisfaction, and demographic characteristics.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Annual incident episodes of LBP were 18.4%. Those who experienced LBP during the past year had a lower baseline perception of general health and were less involved in sporting activities than those free of pain. Those without history of LBP were more likely to be free of back pain after 1 year.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The annual incident episodes of LBP are relatively high and relate indirectly to baseline perception of general health and to level of sporting activities. Those without history of LBP are more likely to be free of back pain after 1 year. These results raise the potential of LBP preventive programs for adult populations.
